Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 19, 2023, AAA announced that the national average for a gallon of gas had decreased by eight cents in the preceding week, reaching $3.56. This price fall occurred despite significant global tensions affecting the oil market, including the escalating Israel-Hamas conflict. The reduction in pump prices was attributed to flat oil prices, which offset the inflationary pressure typically caused by a simultaneous rise in gasoline demand and a tightening of domestic supply. <2> A weekly fuel price report published at the end of September 2023 highlighted the regional differences in gasoline costs across the United States. The report, which provided statistics as of September 25, 2023, showed that the average price for a gallon of gasoline on the East Coast was $3.60. In contrast, the West Coast experienced significantly higher prices, with an average of $5.26 per gallon. The report also detailed prices for other regions, including the Midwest at $3.64, the Gulf Coast at $3.35, and the Rocky Mountain region at $4.00. According to petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan, refinery issues, particularly in Southern California, Arizona, and Nevada, contributed to the elevated prices in the West, while most other states saw prices decrease. <3> California's Division of Petroleum Market Oversight (DPMO) reported that an unusual transaction on the gasoline spot market on September 15, 2023, was a primary driver of a rapid price increase. [1, 2] In a letter to Governor Gavin Newsom and state legislative leaders dated September 22, 2023, the DPMO stated this single transaction caused the market price of gasoline to increase by nearly $0.50 per gallon. [2] The price spike was exacerbated by refinery maintenance for which the industry was inadequately prepared and rising global crude oil prices. [2, 3] The DPMO noted that the effects of the spot market volatility would be felt by consumers at the pump. [1, 2] <4> Hurricane Idalia made landfall as a powerful Category 3 storm in Florida's Big Bend region on August 30, 2023, causing significant damage. The storm brought catastrophic storm surge, with water levels reaching 7 to 12 feet above ground in some coastal communities, and destructive winds. News of the approaching hurricane led to press releases and executive orders from the Florida governor's office starting on August 26, 2023. While Idalia resulted in localized issues, such as gasoline contamination at some stations due to human error before the storm, it did not have a substantial impact on national gas prices. This was because the hurricane's path avoided major oil and gas production hubs. A temporary increase in local demand in Florida was observed, but it did not cause widespread price increases. There were reports of a gas station in Perry, Florida, being destroyed by the hurricane's extreme winds. <5> A fire broke out at Marathon Petroleum's Garyville, Louisiana refinery, the third-largest in the United States, on August 25, 2023. The fire, which originated from a naphtha release in a storage tank, burned for three days and led to the partial shutdown of the facility. In response to the blaze, a mandatory evacuation was issued for residents within a two-mile radius, although this order was lifted later the same day. The incident caused a significant spike in fuel prices, with diesel futures rising by 5% and gasoline futures increasing by about 4%, fueled by concerns over already low distillate stockpiles. While Marathon Petroleum and local authorities maintained that there were no offsite impacts, some residents in the surrounding communities reported health issues such as breathing difficulties and headaches. The fire was extinguished by August 28, 2023. Investigations into the full impact and cause of the fire were subsequently launched. <6> On August 8, 2023, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced it was issuing an emergency fuel waiver to permit the continued sale of E15, a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol, during the summer driving season. [2, 7] This action, which was a 20-day extension of a previous waiver, was intended to increase the available fuel supply and provide consumers with more choices at the pump amidst supply circumstances influenced by the war in Ukraine. [2, 7] The specific waiver was effective from August 10, 2023, through August 29, 2023. [2, 4, 7] <7> An analysis in early August 2023 determined that rising summer gas prices were the result of several factors. [2] The national average price for a gallon of gasoline climbed by about 30 cents in a month to around $3.82. [3] This increase was attributed to a confluence of increased seasonal demand during the summer driving season, a surge in crude oil prices to over $80 per barrel, and significant supply disruptions. [1, 2] These disruptions included production cuts by major oil producers Saudi Arabia and Russia, as well as extreme heatwaves in the U.S. that reduced the operational capacity of refineries in Texas and Louisiana. [1, 2, 4] <8> In early August 2023, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline increased by 11 cents to $3.82. [2] This rise was primarily attributed to the increasing cost of oil and high temperatures impacting refineries. [2] While prices had been stable for the previous six months, they saw a sudden jump of nearly 30 cents in the month leading up to this point. [2] The price surge contributed to broader inflation, with gasoline prices rising 10.6% in August, which accounted for more than half of the 0.6% monthly increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). [1, 5] Despite the increase, some analysts at the time did not expect the national average to reach $4 a gallon, citing the approaching end of the summer driving season and a retreat in oil prices from recent highs. [2] <9> In August 2023, the national average for a gallon of gasoline rose to approximately $3.78, a significant increase of about 25 to 30 cents from the previous month. This atypical summer price hike was attributed to a combination of factors. Extreme heat waves, particularly in Texas and Louisiana, led to unexpected outages and reduced production at several oil refineries. Concurrently, global oil supplies were tightened by production cuts from major oil-producing nations, including Russia and Saudi Arabia, which drove up the price of crude oil. Reports from early August 2023 confirmed these factors as the primary drivers behind the surge in gas prices. <10> The national average for a gallon of regular gasoline surged by 13 cents to $3.71, a development announced by AAA on July 27, 2023. [2, 14] This increase, which followed a period of relative stability in fuel costs, was primarily attributed to a rise in oil prices. [2, 14] In the weeks leading up to the surge, pump prices had seen only minor fluctuations, rising from $3.55 on July 13 to $3.58 on July 20. [2, 14] The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) confirmed the price increase, reporting the average for July 2023 as $3.712 per gallon. [17] By early August, the price had continued to climb, reaching $3.79 by August 9, 2023. [4]

An early August 2025 report mentioned the average price was significantly lower than the $3.47 at the same time in 2024. <8> In late August 2025, the BP Whiting Refinery in Indiana, the largest in the U.S. Midwest, shut down operations due to severe flooding from thunderstorms that occurred on August 19, 2025. The prolonged outage at the 440,000 barrel-per-day facility disrupted a critical source of gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel for the region just ahead of the busy Labor Day travel weekend. As a result, states in the Great Lakes region, including Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Ohio, experienced a significant surge in gasoline prices, with some estimates predicting an increase of 15 to 35 cents per gallon. The refinery began restarting operations a few days after the shutdown and was reported to be back to normal rates by August 27, 2025. <9> The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) reported in its Weekly Petroleum Status Report that U.S. commercial crude oil inventories increased by approximately 3 million barrels for the week ending August 8, 2025. This brought the total commercial crude oil stocks to 426.7 million barrels. The build was contrary to analysts' expectations of a small decrease. Concurrently, crude stocks at the Cushing, Oklahoma delivery hub saw a slight increase of 45,000 barrels. In contrast to the crude oil build, gasoline inventories fell by about 0.8 million barrels, while distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 0.7 million barrels.

This increase, up 29.6% year over year, was largely driven by consumers rushing to take advantage of a federal EV tax credit set to expire at the end of September. While the overall EV market grew, Tesla's market share decreased from 49% in Q3 2024 to 41% in Q3 2025, despite an 8% year-over-year sales gain. Other automakers like General Motors and Volkswagen saw their EV sales more than double. The top-selling EV models for the quarter were the Tesla Model Y and Model 3, followed by the Chevrolet Equinox EV. The legislation, authored by Assemblymember David Alvarez, is intended to lower fuel costs for consumers, diversify the state's fuel supply, and mitigate gasoline price spikes. Prior to the bill's signing, California was the only state where E15 sales were not allowed. The law allows E15 to be sold while the California Air Resources Board (CARB) continues its study on the fuel blend's environmental impact. <9> A U.S. Travel Association forecast projects that the travel sector will experience slower growth in 2025, buoyed by resilience in domestic leisure travel which is expected to grow by 1.9% to $895 billion despite broader economic concerns. In contrast, international inbound travel is anticipated to see its first decrease since 2020, with visits projected to fall by 6.3% to 67.9 million. This decline is largely attributed to a significant reduction in travel from Canada. Domestic business travel is also expected to see muted growth of 1.4%. The association anticipates a resumption of stronger growth in international and business travel in 2026 and beyond, driven by major events hosted in the U.S. such as the FIFA World Cup and America's 250th anniversary.
